transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A national park in Kenya has reported a significant increase in its elephant population over the past decade, thanks to enhanced anti-poaching measures and community conservation programs. The latest wildlife census shows that the elephant population in Amboseli National Park has grown by 40 percent since 2015, from approximately 1,200 to over 1,700 individuals. Park rangers attribute this success to several factors: increased patrols using drone technology, better cooperation with local Maasai communities who help monitor wildlife, and stricter penalties for ivory poaching. The Kenya Wildlife Service has also established specialized anti-poaching units equipped with night-vision goggles and GPS tracking devices. Community outreach programs have been particularly effective, providing education about wildlife conservation and creating economic opportunities through ecotourism that give local residents a stake in protecting elephants rather than harming them. Conservationists caution that challenges remain, including habitat loss due to human population growth and climate change affecting water sources, but describe the population rebound as an encouraging sign that protective measures work.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: A popular ride-sharing company announced this week that it plans to transition its entire fleet to electric vehicles by 2035. The company, which operates in over 60 countries, says the move will help reduce carbon emissions and improve air quality in major cities. Under the new policy, drivers who use gasoline-powered cars will be phased out gradually, with financial incentives offered to those who switch to electric vehicles early. The company has committed 200 million dollars to help drivers purchase EVs through discounted loans and charging infrastructure partnerships. Several cities, including London and Los Angeles, have already implemented low-emission zones that make driving gasoline cars more expensive, providing additional motivation for the transition. Environmental groups have praised the announcement as a positive step, though some critics point out that the timeline is too slow given the urgency of climate change. The company says it will continue investing in autonomous vehicle technology alongside the electric transition.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: A new study published in the Journal of Nutrition suggests that eating breakfast regularly may improve academic performance in school-aged children. Researchers from the University of Texas followed over 5,000 elementary school students for two years, tracking their breakfast habits and comparing them to standardized test scores in math and reading. The findings indicate that children who ate breakfast every day scored an average of 15 percent higher on math tests and 12 percent higher on reading tests compared to those who frequently skipped breakfast. The study also found that regular breakfast eaters had better attendance records and fewer behavioral problems in class. Researchers note that breakfast doesn't have to be elaborate—even a simple meal like whole-grain cereal with fruit or yogurt can provide the glucose and nutrients growing brains need to function optimally in the morning. The study adds to a growing body of evidence supporting school breakfast programs, which many districts have expanded in recent years to ensure all students have access to a morning meal regardless of family income.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Jack): Hi Rachel, I'm glad I caught you. I wanted to ask you about the gym membership—you've been going to that new fitness center downtown, haven't you?
Woman (Rachel): Hi Jack! Yes, I joined about three months ago, and I've been really happy with it. Are you thinking about signing up too?

Man: I'm considering it. The gym at my university is okay, but it gets really crowded in the afternoons, and the equipment is pretty old. I've also been wanting to try some classes—spinning, yoga, that kind of thing. Do they offer a good variety?

Woman: They have a huge range of classes, actually. They do spinning and yoga, as you mentioned, plus HIIT classes, Pilates, kickboxing, and even dance workouts like Zumba. Most classes are included with membership, though a few of the specialized ones like reformer Pilates cost extra. The nice thing is they have classes early in the morning before work, at lunchtime, and in the evenings, so there's usually something that fits your schedule.
Man: That sounds great. What about the cost? I remember hearing gym memberships can be pretty expensive in this city.

Woman: It depends on the plan. The basic monthly membership is 45 pounds, which gives you access to the gym floor and standard classes during off-peak hours—before 4 PM on weekdays and all day weekends. If you want anytime access including peak hours, it's 60 pounds a month. There's also an annual membership option that works out cheaper per month, but you have to pay for the whole year upfront.

Man: I see. I'd probably need the anytime access since my classes are mostly in the mornings, so I'd go in the late afternoon or evening. Do they have personal trainers available? I've been thinking about getting some help with a workout routine.

Woman: They do, but personal training sessions are separate from membership—they're about 40 pounds per hour, which I think is pretty standard. However, they do offer free fitness inductions when you join, where a trainer shows you how to use all the equipment safely and helps you create a basic workout plan. That might be enough to get you started.
Man: That's good to know. I think I'll go take a tour this weekend. Thanks for the information, Rachel!
Woman: No problem! If you do join, maybe we can go to a spinning class together sometime.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Female)
paras: The history of chocolate begins more than 3,000 years ago in Mesoamerica, where ancient civilizations including the Maya and Aztec cultivated cacao trees and created a bitter, frothy beverage from cacao beans mixed with water, spices, and chili peppers. Unlike the sweet chocolate we know today, this ancient drink was considered sacred and was used in religious ceremonies, as well as serving as a form of currency. When Spanish explorers arrived in the Americas in the 16th century, they brought cacao back to Europe, where it gradually became popular among the aristocracy after sugar and cinnamon were added to make it sweeter. The Industrial Revolution brought major changes to chocolate production. In 1828, a Dutch chemist named Coenraad van Houten invented a press that could separate cocoa butter from roasted cacao beans, creating cocoa powder and making chocolate cheaper to produce on a large scale. Later in the 19th century, Swiss innovators developed milk chocolate by adding condensed milk to the chocolate mixture, and Rodolphe Lindt invented the conching process, which creates the smooth, creamy texture we associate with modern chocolate. Today, chocolate is produced and consumed worldwide, with major growing regions in West Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia. However, the chocolate industry faces significant challenges, including concerns about child labor on cacao farms, deforestation associated with cacao cultivation, and fair compensation for small-scale farmers who grow most of the world's cacao despite earning very little from the multi-billion-dollar industry. Many companies are now working to develop more sustainable and ethical supply chains in response to consumer demand for responsibly produced chocolate.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Male)
paras: Public transportation systems are often called the backbone of major cities, enabling millions of people to travel to work, school, and other destinations each day. Well-designed public transit offers numerous benefits beyond simply moving people from place to place. One of the most significant advantages is environmental: buses, trains, and subways can carry dozens or even hundreds of passengers at once, dramatically reducing per-person carbon emissions compared to private cars. Public transit also reduces traffic congestion, which saves time for all road users and reduces the need for expensive new highway construction. For individuals, using public transportation can be significantly cheaper than owning and maintaining a car, potentially saving thousands of dollars per year on car payments, insurance, gas, and parking. Good public transit also improves accessibility for people who cannot drive, including teenagers, elderly individuals, and people with disabilities, allowing them to participate more fully in community life. Despite these benefits, many public transit systems face challenges. Aging infrastructure in many cities requires costly repairs and upgrades. Some systems struggle with reliability issues, including delays and overcrowding during peak hours. Funding is another persistent challenge, as public transit rarely covers its operating costs through fares alone and requires government subsidies. Recent developments offer hope for improvement: many cities are investing in bus rapid transit systems, modernizing subway lines, and integrating contactless payment systems to make riding public transit more convenient. Some cities are also experimenting with free-fare zones in downtown areas to encourage ridership and reduce traffic.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Learning a second language in adulthood can be challenging, but research shows it offers numerous cognitive and practical benefits that make the effort worthwhile. While it is true that children tend to acquire languages more easily than adults, adult learners bring certain advantages to the process, including better metalinguistic awareness, larger vocabularies in their native language, and more developed learning strategies. Studies have consistently shown that bilingual adults demonstrate better executive function—they are better at switching between tasks, ignoring distractions, and resolving conflicting information compared to monolingual adults. This enhanced cognitive control appears to come from the constant mental exercise of selecting the appropriate language for a given situation while suppressing the other. Long-term research also suggests that bilingualism may contribute to better cognitive reserve in older age, delaying the onset of dementia symptoms by several years on average. Professionally, speaking a second language can be a significant career advantage in our increasingly globalized economy, opening up job opportunities in international business, education, healthcare, translation, tourism, and many other fields. People who speak multiple languages also often report enjoying deeper connections with other cultures, whether through travel, literature, films, or conversations with people from different backgrounds. Experts recommend that adult language learners prioritize consistent practice over long, intensive study sessions, seek out opportunities for real conversation with native speakers rather than relying solely on textbooks, and embrace making mistakes as a natural part of the learning process. With motivation and regular practice, adults can achieve high levels of proficiency in a new language at any age.
